transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE), Ben Chu (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Meridian CTO), Ravi Kumar (Meridian SRE), Sam Lee (Meridian Product), Tina (Meridian Legal)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Walkthrough of org/project key patterns for multi-tenant rate limiting and quota enforcement.
- Discussed tradeoffs between hosted API, Dedicated reservation, and VPC/private deployment for Meridian's compliance needs.
- Agreed to run a Dedicated trial with benchmark tests and provide traffic traces.

Topics: org keys, project keys, rate shaping, concurrency quotas, fairburst, throttling strategies, routing fallbacks, cadence for pilot

Transcript body:
00:00 - Alice Park: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off in a minute, appreciate you making time. Quick roll call?
00:12 - Maya Patel: Hi this is Maya, sorry for joining a tad late, CTO at Meridian.
00:16 - Ravi Kumar: Ravi here, SRE.
00:18 - Sam Lee: Sam from Product.
00:20 - Alice Park: Great thanks, Ben I'll hand to you for the technical demo and the org/project key playbook.
00:25 - Ben Chu: Cool thanks Alice. So the agenda is: show our console routing and quota UI, then go into example org/project key mappings and a demo of a fairburst + backpressure scenario, and then Q&A. We'll also cover Dedicated trial and what we recommend for compliance.
00:42 - Ben Chu: Quick note -- when we say org key we mean the top-level identifier we use to apply org-wide quotas and RBAC. Projects are child keys to segment teams/features.
01:05 - Sam Lee: Can you show us how we'd map our existing API keys? We have platform tokens and team tokens today.
01:12 - Ben Chu: Yup, we can import existing keys or mint new project-scoped keys. Example: import your platform token to the org scope, then create project keys for ingestion, realtime, and reporting. You can attach quota policies to either org or project level.
01:35 - Maya Patel: Our main ask is isolating noisy tenants, we saw spikes from one team wrecking the 95th on others. How granular can rules be?
01:44 - Ben Chu: You can set concurrency quotas, token/second, and monthly or daily quotas. We also support custom metrics for bursting, e.g., a leaky-bucket window for short spikes.
02:05 - Ben Chu: I'll share the console -- show org policies > add policy > "Priority lanes". You can create lanes like 'critical', 'standard', 'best-effort' and map project keys to lanes. The runtime enforces by tagging requests with lane and applying fairshare.
02:32 - (screen share) Ben Chu: here's an example policy for a team that needs low latency - they get reserved concurrency on Dedicated pools. If capacity's low, we automatically route to a cheaper model variant or fallback region depending on your policy.
03:10 - Ravi Kumar: Routing to cheaper model variants, does that change output quality? We need to keep regression risk low.
03:18 - Ben Chu: Good question. We recommend using similar model families for fallbacks and running eval sets. Redwood Optimize can monitor quality regressions and alert if outputs diverge beyond a threshold.
03:35 - Maya Patel: How about data residency and VPC - we are in finance and need logs in our VPC and customer-managed KMS?
03:44 - Alice Park: For Private deployments we offer a customer-controlled control plane and KMS integrations. Audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM. We'll include SOC2 summary + VPC checklist after the call.
04:05 - Sam Lee: Ok, show us the quota expression language, like can we do rate by endpoint path?
04:12 - Ben Chu: Yes, limits can be keyed by api path, model, or header. Polices are expression-based - e.g., if header x-team==billing apply project key Y's quota.
04:30 - (minor cross-talk)
04:45 - Ben Chu: Now I'll simulate a noisy tenant with a burst: watch the 95th latency panel and the queue depth.
05:00 - (simulation)
05:20 - Ben Chu: During the simulated spike you can see our backpressure mechanism enqueue requests, apply a tenant-level concurrency cap, and then shed load with 429s for best-effort lane while critical lane keeps throughput.
05:40 - Ravi Kumar: Do you allow token-level sticky routing? We want certain tokens always served by Dedicated hosts for compliance.
05:48 - Ben Chu: Yes - sticky routing by key is available; you can pin keys to Dedicated pools or regions. We persist mapping in the control plane and the runtime honors it.
06:12 - Maya Patel: How do you handle KV cache and prefix caching across model variants? We use heavy caching for chat history.
06:22 - Ben Chu: We have prefix/KV cache that is per-model and can be shared across compatible variants. For private deployments, you can tune cache affinity and TTL. Note: some transcription may show 'KV cash' in some notes, but it's KV cache.
06:45 - Sam Lee: There's an internal concern that if we shard keys a lot we'll explode billing and manageability. Any best-practices?
06:52 - Ben Chu: We suggest an org+project pattern: use 1 org key per company, then up to dozens of project keys for major product lines. Avoid creating keys per user; instead use project keys + user id in headers for downstream attribution. That keeps quota surface manageable.
07:20 - Alice Park: Also you can use aliasing - create temporary tenant keys for short-lived jobs and auto-revoke after. That helps with burst scenarios without permanent key sprawl.
07:36 - Maya Patel: If we pin to Dedicated, what's the billing model? Flat reserve vs burst?
07:44 - Alice Park: Dedicated is reserved capacity. You commit to a monthly pool size; we also offer controlled burst credits for short peaks. We'll share specific pricing tiers in the follow-up.
07:58 - Ravi Kumar: For the trial can we run a real workload with a holdback experiment and see lat/throughput?
08:04 - Ben Chu: Absolutely - Ben will coordinate a benchmark run. We usually ask for a week of traffic traces and a 48hr focused run. We'll run client-side load and collect p95/p99.
08:20 - (screen share) Ben Chu: Console demo - here's the policy editor. You can set token/sec and concurrency caps per project. Example policy: {policy: 'reporting-heavy', concurrency: 8, rate: 40 rps, lane: 'standard'}.
08:48 - Sam Lee: There's also mention of 'fairburst' in the docs; can you explain?
08:56 - Ben Chu: Fairburst allows short bursts above baseline while preserving fairness across tenants. It's a leaky-bucket window we enforce. Busted tenants are throttle-limited to the window.
09:12 - Maya Patel: What about cross-tenant caching? We can't share sensitive prefixes between tenants.
09:20 - Ben Chu: Cache is isolated by default by org and project. You can enable shared caches only where teams opt-in. For PII-sensitive contexts, we recommend per-tenant caches and strict TTLs.
09:39 - Tina (Legal): Quick legal Q - will logs contain user prompt text? We need to redact or keep prompts internal.
09:47 - Alice Park: Logs can be configured. By default we redact sensitive fields from control plane logs; customers on Private can fully control what is logged to their SIEM. We'll send the log schema so you can confirm.
10:08 - Ravi Kumar: If we need to enforce SSO + RBAC for the console and API, what's supported?
10:15 - Alice Park: SSO via SAML/OIDC, plus RBAC with roles: admin, ops, viewer. Token issuance can be restricted to roles. We'll include SSO setup steps and example SAML metadata.
10:35 - Ben Chu: Now I'll trigger a policy change live: moving a project from standard to critical lane - watch the concurrency allocation shift.
10:44 - (live change)
10:58 - Ben Chu: You can see the allocation bumped up, requests in critical lane passed through while best-effort got throttled.
11:12 - Sam Lee: Nice. If an org-level quota blocks a project, can project-level overrides exist?
11:18 - Ben Chu: Yes - policies are hierarchical: org policies apply first, then project overrides. We evaluate the intersection and enforce the stricter constraint unless you set override permissions.
11:35 - Maya Patel: We run some nightly batch jobs that need large token volumes but they can run at off-peak. Can we schedule quota windows?
11:45 - Ben Chu: Yes, scheduled windows and capacity reservations are supported. You can grant a nightly bulk window with higher limits between 02:00-06:00.
12:05 - Alice Park: A common pattern is to reserve burst credits for nightly jobs and use fairburst for daytime interactive traffic.
12:18 - Ravi Kumar: What telemetry do you provide for debugging throttling? We need request ids, token id, and the applied policy id.
12:26 - Ben Chu: Every response includes a trace header with policy id, lane, and decision. Console traces and per-token audit logs are available for Dedicated and Private.
12:42 - (short pause)
13:00 - Ben Chu: I'll flip over to the Optimize recommendations briefly. Optimize analyses latency/cost tradeoffs and suggests quantization and batching levels per workload. For example, if you run many short requests, Optimize might recommend smaller batch sizes but aggressive KV prefix caching.
13:24 - Sam Lee: Can Optimize recommend model variants for fallbacks?
13:30 - Ben Chu: Yes, it suggests model family variants with expected quality delta and cost delta. You can set a quality window to avoid regressions.
13:46 - Maya Patel: For compliance we need model provenance logged. Does Redwood record which model variant served each request?
:13:52 - Ben Chu: Yes, model id and commit metadata are in the audit logs.
14:10 - Ravi Kumar: Any limits on number of project keys?
14:15 - Ben Chu: Practically no hard limit, but we recommend keeping under a few hundred for manageability; if you need thousands we can discuss an automated key namespace strategy.
14:30 - Sam Lee: Are quota updates eventual or immediate? We changed a policy last week on our test env and it took a bit to apply.
14:38 - Ben Chu: Policy changes are pushed to control plane and then to runtime with near-real-time propagation (seconds to low tens of seconds). In Dedicated there are options for immediate enforced rollout.
14:55 - Maya Patel: On fallback routing, do you do model conversion or only select compatible variants?
15:02 - Ben Chu: Only compatible variants. We avoid conversions that change tokenization or embeddings. Runtime enforces compatibility matrix.
15:20 - Ravi Kumar: What about rate enforcement on long-running streams?
15:25 - Ben Chu: Streaming requests can be throttled by token emission rate or by active connection count. We have streaming-specific quotas.
15:40 - (noise, someone types)
16:00 - Alice Park: Quick pause for questions from Legal. Tina?
16:05 - Tina: Just to confirm - for Private deployment are we able to audit code changes and have a hardened release schedule?
16:12 - Lina Ortiz: Yes, Private deployments have a hardened release cadence and we can provide signed release notes and attestations.
16:25 - Maya Patel: For the Dedicated trial, will we be able to route a subset of production traffic?
16:32 - Ben Chu: Yes you can mirror or shadow a subset first; we recommend 10-20% mirrored requests for initial validation before moving traffic live.
16:50 - Ravi Kumar: Regarding cost controls - can we set hard spend limits per project?
16:56 - Ben Chu: You can set quota caps that effectively limit spend and have alerting thresholds; we also support programmatic budget locks for emergency cutoffs.
17:12 - Sam Lee: Can you demo the billing view per project?
17:16 - (screen share) Ben Chu: Here's the cost breakdown by project and model variant, token counts, and estimated $ per 1M tokens.
17:45 - Sam Lee: If we shard keys across environments (staging/prod), will analytics still aggregate?
17:50 - Ben Chu: Yes, the console can roll up by org or by tag. We recommend tagging keys with env:prod or env:staging for rollups.
18:05 - Maya Patel: Any known limitations with our stack (we're on Kubernetes, private VPC with strict egress)?
18:14 - Ben Chu: Kubernetes + VPC is a common setup. For private deployments you'll need to open specific ports to the runtime, and we support egress-lockdown patterns. We'll include a network diagram in the follow-up.
18:32 - Ravi Kumar: For large batches we prefer GPU pinned instances. Do you support pinning workloads to instance types?
18:39 - Ben Chu: Yes, Dedicated pools can be configured with specific GPU families and we let you reserve them. Batching strategy will adapt to hardware.
19:02 - (short pause)
19:20 - Alice Park: Ok let's walk through an example policy doc - Ben?
19:24 - Ben Chu: Example: Org policy: global 500 rps and org concurrency 400. Project "ingest" override: concurrency 200, rate 300 rps, lane critical reserved 30% of pool. Nightly window 02:00-05:00 gives ingest 2x rate.
19:50 - Sam Lee: How do you handle sudden token theft or leaked keys?
19:56 - Ben Chu: You can rotate keys automatically, set usage alerts, and set emergency revoke rules. There's also per-key IP allowlist.
20:12 - Maya Patel: We'd want an integration to our PagerDuty for throttling incident alerts.
20:19 - Ben Chu: We have webhooks and Ops integrations for alerts, and can push to PagerDuty, Slack, or a SIEM.
20:38 - Alice Park: I'm going to summarize next steps. We'll send: pricing + playbook, SOC2 summary & VPC checklist, dedicated trial provisioning steps, and a benchmark script. Ben will follow up on scheduling the benchmark.
20:55 - Sam Lee: Two quick follow-ups - can we get a sample policy JSON and a list of telemetry fields?
21:02 - Ben Chu: Yes, sample policy JSON and telemetry schema will be attached to the follow-up email.
21:20 - Maya Patel: Also include a note around how Optimize measures quality deltas so our compliance team can review.
21:30 - Alice Park: We'll include that.
21:40 - (wrap-up)
21:50 - Alice Park: Thanks everyone. We'll send the materials and aim to have the trial ready by next week pending your traces.
22:00 - Maya Patel: Thanks, appreciate it.
22:05 - Ravi Kumar: Thanks all.
22:10 - Sam Lee: Bye.
22:20 - (call ends)

Post-call notes (auto):
- Customer prioritized: noisy-tenant isolation, pinned routing for compliance, and predictable economics.
- Risks: Meridian requires strict log redaction & KMS; private deployment likely needed if logs must remain internal.
- Good fit: Redwood's Dedicated + Private options and Optimize toolkit align with needs.

End of transcript.
